confirmed.title: 360Learning API key transmitted as a URL query parameter instead of an Authorization header
confirmed.evidence: url.searchParams.set('apiKey', env.LMS_360L_API_KEY ?? '') puts the live LMS secret into the request URL's query string. The InfoSearch sibling client correctly uses `authorization: Bearer ...` (infosearch-client.ts:60). Query strings are routinely captured by reverse proxies, CDNs, APM (the codebase ships dd-trace), and any HTTP debug logging — none of which the Pino redact list (logger.ts:60-79, which only redacts header paths and `*.apiKey`/`*.token` object keys, not a secret embedded inside a URL string) will scrub. Verified the secret does NOT leak via the thrown error message (undici reports 'fetch failed' / 'aborted' without the URL), so this is exposure-surface hardening, not a confirmed leak.
confirmed.fix: Send the key in an Authorization/x-api-key header per the 360Learning auth contract (the TODO already flags verifying the real header), matching the InfoSearch client; keep secrets out of URLs.

verdict.reason: CONFIRMED. apps/api/src/lib/lms-360learning.ts:57-58 builds `new URL(\`${base}/api/v2/courses\`)` then `url.searchParams.set('apiKey', env.LMS_360L_API_KEY ?? '')`, and fetch(url, ...) at line 64 transmits the live LMS API key in the request URL's query string with no Authorization header. The secret is real: env.ts:115 defines LMS_360L_API_KEY as a required credential when the integration is enabled (env.ts:209-210), not a dev stub. The sibling client does it correctly — infosearch-client.ts:60 uses `authorization: Bearer ${env.INFOSEARCH_API_KEY}` — confirming the query-param choice is an inconsistency, not a deliberate API requirement (the file's own TODO at lines 9-12 admits the auth header is unverified against the 360Learning docs). No guard in the call chain mitigates the URL-embedded case: the Pino redact list (logger.ts:60-79) only covers header paths and object keys named apiKey/token/etc., none of which match a secret living as a substring inside a URL object's href/search; and dd-trace is shipped and initialized with `plugins: true` + HTTP auto-instrumentation (datadog.ts:48-59) with no urlFilter/query-string scrubbing, so outbound HTTP-client spans tag http.url with the full query string by default, capturing the apiKey in APM. The claim is also honest about scope: the thrown LmsError message (lines 70-72) wraps undici's generic err.message ('fetch failed'/'aborted') which does not embed the URL, so this is exposure-surface hardening, not a confirmed runtime leak. Query strings are routinely captured by reverse proxies, CDNs, browser/server access logs, and APM — a recognized anti-pattern for secret transmission.

confirmed.title: API-key callers get coarse read/write scopes that unlock settings:write and org-settings:write — access-group reconfiguration via an org key
confirmed.evidence: For role 'api', requirePermission collapses EVERY '*:write' permission to a single 'write' scope check. The new admin surfaces user-groups.ts (settings:write — create/edit access groups, set scopeAll=true to widen visibility) and org-settings.ts (settings:write — opportunity filter rules) are now reachable by any API key holding the generic 'write' scope, even one provisioned only to e.g. write bid scores. access-scope.ts:24 also treats every apikey:<id> principal as unrestricted, so an over-scoped key both reconfigures the scope model and is itself exempt from it. Pre-existing collapse logic, but commit 46c98a16/921293ce added the new privileged routes that ride it. No cross-tenant break (orgId is taken from the key row), so this is intra-org least-privilege, not tenant isolation.
confirmed.fix: Map fine-grained PermissionKeys to per-key scope strings (or restrict settings:write/org-settings:write to user principals only) so a write-scoped integration key cannot reconfigure access groups or org filter rules.

verdict.reason:
VERIFIED REAL against the actual code. The full exploit chain holds at every cited point:

1. apps/api/src/plugins/rbac.ts:50-54 — For role 'api', requirePermission collapses EVERY '*:write' permission to one generic 'write' scope check: `const requiredScope = permission.endsWith(':write') ? 'write' : 'read'; if (req.auth.scopes.includes(requiredScope)) return;`. There is no per-resource scope. Confirmed verbatim.

2. The two new privileged surfaces ride that collapse with NO second guard:
   - apps/api/src/routes/user-groups.ts:127,176,229,260,300 — all mutations gated ONLY by `server.requirePermission('settings:write')` (create/edit access groups, set scopeAll=true).
   - apps/api/src/routes/org-settings.ts:40 — PUT /org-settings/opportunity-filters gated ONLY by `server.requirePermission('settings:write')`.
   - Contrast: apps/api/src/routes/roles.ts:81,142,246 pairs the SAME permission with `server.requireRole('admin')`, which an api caller fails (role 'api' is not in allowed and has no UserRole rows). The two new routes omit that admin role guard, so they ARE reachable by a write-scoped API key while the roles routes are not. This asymmetry is the crux.

3. Both routes are registered and reachable: server.routes.ts:139 (orgSettingsRoutes) and :186 (userGroupRoutes).

4. The scope model is coarse with no granularity: API keys are created at apps/api/src/routes/dust-integration.ts:240-245 validating scopes as z.enum(['read','write','mcp']). 'write' is the only write-class scope, so a key provisioned to write anything (e.g. bid scores) holds the exact 'write' that unlocks settings:write. auth.ts:322-327 sets role:'api' and scopes:apiKey.scopes directly from the key row.

5. access-scope.ts:24/53 confirmed — apikey:<id> principals fail UUID_RE and return { unrestricted: true }, so an over-scoped key is itself exempt from the scope model it can reconfigure (it can create a scopeAll=true group to widen visibility).

6. Tenant isolation is intact — orgId comes from the key row (auth.ts:323) and every mutation is audit-logged — so this is an intra-org least-privilege / privilege-escalation defect, not a tenant-isolation break. Commit attribution also checks out: git log shows 46c98a16 and 921293ce introduced user-groups.ts and org-settings.ts.

Severity note: 'minor' is defensible (requires an already-issued write key, same-tenant only, fully audit-logged), but a narrowly-scoped write key being able to reconfigure the org's data-visibility scope model is a real intra-org privilege escalation, so I'd place it at the minor/moderate boundary. Fix: add server.requireRole('admin') to the user-groups and org-settings mutations (matching roles.ts), and/or stop collapsing settings:write to the generic 'write' scope for api callers — e.g. require an explicit 'admin'/'settings' scope rather than the catch-all 'write'.

confirmed.title: InfoSearch activity webhook egresses the viewer's email to the external system on every account view
confirmed.evidence: notifyInfoSearchActivity sends `actor: input.userEmail` (the authenticated user's email, infosearch.ts:43) to the external InfoSearch MCP via a fire-and-forget log_activity call. This is unconditional PII egress to a third party on every /infosearch/leads request, gated only by the integration being configured. The route does not record consent or scope this; combined with the unscoped account param (finding 1), it both reads cross-scope intel and reports who looked at it to an outside service.
confirmed.fix: Confirm the InfoSearch usage-logging requirement actually requires the real email (vs an opaque actor id), and document the PII egress in the integration's data-flow; consider sending a stable user id rather than the raw email.

verdict.reason:
Verified real at the cited code. Chain confirmed end to end:

1) infosearch.ts:43 calls notifyInfoSearchActivity({ account: req.query.account, userEmail: req.auth.email ?? null }) unconditionally after a successful fetchInfoSearchLeads. There is no consent gate, no per-user opt-out, and no permission/scope check around the egress.

2) req.auth.email is the AUTHENTICATED VIEWER's email. AuthContext.email (apps/api/src/plugins/auth.ts:38) is populated from the Clerk JWT `email` claim in production (auth.ts:107, 278) or from the seed user in stub mode (auth.ts:75). The route is an authenticated route (onRequest hook sets req.auth for any route lacking config:{public:true}; infosearch route does not opt out), so the value is the requesting user's work email.

3) infosearch-client.ts:107-123 — notifyInfoSearchActivity issues a fire-and-forget JSON-RPC `tools/call` -> `log_activity` with `actor: input.userEmail` to the external InfoSearch MCP at env.INFOSEARCH_MCP_URL (rpc() at lines 49-77). So the viewer's email does leave the system to a third party on every successful /infosearch/leads request.

4) The only guard is infosearchConfigured() (route line 40; client lines 42-47), which checks INFOSEARCH_ENABLED==='true' and that URL+key are set — exactly "gated only by the integration being configured," as the claim states.

No upstream guard (Zod schema, rbac preHandler, query-guard, requirePermission, normalizeName) blocks or scopes this PII egress. The querystring schema (infosearch.ts:35) only validates `account`; it does not touch the email path.

Severity held at minor (matches the claimed rating): the egress is real PII to a third party, BUT (a) the recipient is an org-configured, Bearer-authenticated vendor MCP the tenant explicitly enabled, not an arbitrary endpoint, and (b) the route header comment (infosearch.ts:2-3) documents it as intended ("per the demo brief's usage-logging requirement"). It is a deliberate first-party-to-configured-vendor activity log, which caps severity at minor; the absence of a consent record / per-user opt-out is the legitimate residual concern. The claim's "compounding with finding 1 (unscoped account)" framing is auxiliary, but the standalone email-egress fact is verified independently.

confirmed.title: Account cockpit health score counts the WHOLE org's contacts and tasks on the dashboard path, so the same account shows two different scores
confirmed.evidence: buildCockpit computes `health: computeSignalCoverage({ company, contacts, openDeals, tasks })`. `openDeals` is filtered to the company (line 475), but `contacts` and `tasks` are the raw function parameters. In the dashboard path (dashboard.service.ts:314-322) those parameters are the FULL org lists (contact.findMany take:200, task.findMany take:100, no company filter). So computeSignalCoverage's contact factor (`Math.min(40, contacts.length*10)`, withEmail ratio, influence>=4 check) and engagement factor (recent/onTrack tasks) are computed over EVERY company in the org, not the selected one. The per-company endpoint buildCompanyCockpit (dashboard.queries.ts:241,256) pre-filters contacts/tasks by `customer: company.name`, so GET /crm/companies/:id returns the correct per-company score while the main dashboard cockpit returns an org-wide-inflated score for the identical account. keyContacts/recentActivity in the same builder DO filter by `contact.customer === company.name` (lines 631,646), proving the contacts arg was meant to be scoped before scoring.
confirmed.fix: Filter contacts and tasks to the company before passing them to computeSignalCoverage, e.g. `const companyContacts = contacts.filter(c => c.customer === company.name); const companyTasks = tasks.filter(t => t.opportunity?.customer === company.name);` and pass those. This makes the dashboard path agree with buildCompanyCockpit.

verdict.reason:
CONFIRMED at every cited location. dashboard.cockpit.ts:629 calls computeSignalCoverage({ company, contacts, openDeals, tasks }). openDeals is company-scoped (line 475 filters companyOpps), but `contacts` and `tasks` are the raw buildCockpit parameters with no per-company filter. computeSignalCoverage (cockpit.ts:92-147) computes the contact factor over the entire `contacts` array (`Math.min(40, contacts.length*10)`, withEmail ratio, influence>=4) and the engagement factor over the entire `tasks` array (recent/open/onTrack), never re-scoping internally.

Dashboard path (dashboard.service.ts): contacts = prisma.contact.findMany({ where: { orgId, deletedAt: null }, take: 200 }) at lines 110-124; tasks = prisma.task.findMany({ where: { orgId, deletedAt: null }, take: 100 }) at lines 125-138 — both org-wide, no company filter. These exact arrays are passed into buildCockpit at lines 314-322.

Per-company path (dashboard.queries.ts): buildCompanyCockpit loads contacts via where: { orgId, customer: company.name } (line 241) and tasks via where: { orgId, opportunity: { customer: company.name } } (line 256), then calls the SAME buildCockpit (line 307). So GET /crm/companies/:id returns a correctly-scoped per-company health score while the main dashboard cockpit returns an org-wide-inflated score for the identical account — two different scores for one account.

Internal-inconsistency proof holds: the same builder scopes keyContacts by contact.customer === company.name (line 631) and recentActivity by task.opportunity?.customer === company.name (line 646), showing the contacts/tasks args were intended to be company-scoped before scoring but the health call uses the unscoped arrays.

No guard mitigates it: orgId multi-tenancy is intact, but nothing scopes contacts/tasks to the selected company on the dashboard path before the health computation. Severity stays major: the cross-endpoint discrepancy is real and user-visible (same account, two scores) and the data is genuinely incorrect/inflated. It is not critical because firmographics (the heaviest 0.3 weight) and the pipeline factor are correctly scoped, and the two corrupted factors saturate (contacts cap at 4, recent tasks cap at 3), so in a populated org they typically peg at their maxima rather than swing wildly — a wrong-but-bounded inflation, not arbitrary corruption.

confirmed.title: M7 access scoping silently hides opportunities due to country-code case mismatch (group codes uppercased, opportunity.country stored raw)
confirmed.evidence: applyOpportunityScope filters with `{ country: { in: scope.countries } }`. scope.countries come from UserGroup.scopeCountries which are forced uppercase by the CountryCode schema (`.trim().toUpperCase().regex(/^[A-Z]{2}$/)`, packages/shared/src/schemas/user-groups.ts:9-13). But opportunity.country is validated only as `z.string().max(2).nullable()` (packages/shared/src/schemas/opportunity.ts:71) — NO case normalization — and stored verbatim (`country: body.country ?? null`, apps/api/src/routes/opportunities.mutations.ts:120). An opportunity created with country 'fr'/'Fr' is therefore never matched by a group scoped to ['FR'], so a restricted user loses visibility of opportunities they are entitled to see (and the matching `{country:{in:[...]}}` is a silent filter, not an error). The same raw `body.country` is used case-sensitively for the territory lookup at opportunities.mutations.ts:56 (`countryCodes: { has: body.country }`), compounding the inconsistency.
confirmed.fix: Normalize opportunity country to uppercase ISO-2 at the schema/write layer (add `.trim().toUpperCase()` to the opportunity country field, matching CountryCode), or uppercase both sides of the comparison in applyOpportunityScope. Backfill existing rows.

verdict.reason:
VERIFIED REAL. The asymmetric normalization is exactly as claimed and is live on the LIST/COUNT scoping path.

Chain confirmed against actual code:
1. apps/api/src/lib/access-scope.ts:108 — applyOpportunityScope emits `{ country: { in: scope.countries } }` inside an OR (with territory.countryCodes hasSome and ownerId). It is a silent filter, not an error. It IS wired live: opportunities.ts:44-48 (LIST) and :155-159 (COUNT) call getAccessScope + applyOpportunityScope.
2. scope.countries derive from UserGroup.scopeCountries (access-scope.ts:71). Those are forced uppercase by CountryCode = z.string().trim().toUpperCase().regex(/^[A-Z]{2}$/) at packages/shared/src/schemas/user-groups.ts:9-13, applied on both UserGroupCreate (line 45) and UserGroupPatch (line 53). So stored group codes are guaranteed uppercase.
3. opportunity.country is validated only as z.string().max(2).nullable() at packages/shared/src/schemas/opportunity.ts:71 — NO case normalization. OpportunityCreate (line 81) and OpportunityImport (line 113) inherit it unchanged.
4. Stored verbatim: country: body.country ?? null at opportunities.mutations.ts:120 (create) and :351 (import); PATCH writes req.body.country verbatim at opportunities.ts:362. A grep for toUpperCase/normalize in the mutations file returned zero matches — no normalization guard exists.
5. DB confirms case-sensitivity: schema.prisma:417 country String? @db.VarChar(2) (Postgres VarChar is case-sensitive) and the opps_org_country_idx index on (orgId, country) is likewise case-sensitive — nothing folds case at the DB layer either.

Consequence: an opportunity created/imported with 'fr' or 'Fr' is never matched by a group scoped to ['FR']. A restricted, non-owner user whose territory also doesn't match loses visibility of opportunities they are entitled to see — a silent access-scoping defect (under-exposure, not over-exposure, so security-wise it leaks nothing, but it hides entitled data). The compounding territory inconsistency at opportunities.mutations.ts:58 (countryCodes: { has: body.country }) is also accurate — territory codes are not normalized at write either, so case mismatch can also break auto-territory assignment.

Severity major is appropriate: it does not over-expose data, but it produces incorrect, hard-to-diagnose visibility gaps for restricted users on the sensitive commercial dataset, depending entirely on uncontrolled input casing. EVIDENCE line references are all exact and correct.

confirmed.title: Spotlight Ref ingestion stores accountKey un-normalized while the read route normalizes it — references silently never surface
confirmed.evidence: ingestProjectReference (the only writer) persists `accountKey: input.accountKey` with NO normalizeName(). The read route filters with `accountKey: normalizeName(req.query.accountKey)` (apps/api/src/routes/project-references.ts:66). Every sibling account feature normalizes on BOTH sides — cross-sell (cross-sell.ts:111 create, :85 read) and governance (governance.ts:140 create, :114 read). Today the seed happens to pass a pre-normalized literal ('ci-financial', packages/db/src/seed.ts:332), masking the bug, but any ingestion that passes a display name like 'CI Financial' stores 'CI Financial' and the cockpit's normalized lookup ('ci-financial') will never match, so validated references disappear from the account view with no error.
confirmed.fix: Normalize on write: `accountKey: normalizeName(input.accountKey)` in ingestProjectReference, matching the cross-sell/governance writers.

verdict.reason:
VERIFIED REAL (latent bug, severity minor — correctly classified). Every link in the claim holds against the actual code:

1. Writer does not normalize — apps/api/src/services/project-reference.service.ts:25 stores `accountKey: input.accountKey` with no normalizeName(). ingestProjectReference is the documented sole ingestion seam (file header lines 1-8); there is no public create route.

2. Reader normalizes — apps/api/src/routes/project-references.ts:66 filters with `accountKey: normalizeName(req.query.accountKey)`.

3. normalizeName is non-trivial — apps/api/src/services/crm/dashboard.utils.ts:158-164 trims, lowercases, collapses non-alphanumeric runs to `-`, strips edge hyphens. So a display name 'CI Financial' would be stored verbatim by the writer but looked up as 'ci-financial' by the reader, never matching. Asymmetry is real.

4. Siblings normalize on BOTH sides (confirmed by grep): governance.ts:140 (create) + :114 (read); cross-sell.ts:111 (create) + :85 (read). The project-reference writer is the lone deviation from the established account-feature pattern.

5. Masked today, as claimed: the seed writes `accountKey: 'ci-financial'` (packages/db/src/seed.ts:332, via createMany — not even through the service), and the integration test uses `ACCOUNT = 'governance-test-account'` (governance.integration.test.ts:13) passed pre-normalized on both write (ingestProjectReference) and read (?accountKey=...). Both literals are already in normalized form, so no test can catch the write/read asymmetry.

Severity confirmation: minor is correct, not under/over-stated. The writer is an explicit STUB (header: 'intentionally NOT exposed as a public create route'); the live Spotlight Ref ingestion trigger that would pass display names does not exist yet ('lands with the Spotlight Ref rework'). So there is currently no production code path that can trigger the silent-disappearance, but the writer's contract genuinely accepts un-normalized accountKey while the only reader normalizes — a real, untested latent correctness defect that will bite when ingestion is wired up. No severity adjustment warranted.

confirmed.title: Key-accounts list silently undercounts pipeline stats past the 1000-opportunity ceiling
confirmed.evidence: GET /accounts/key fetches up to `limit` companies (querystring max 200), then aggregates their opportunities with `prisma.opportunity.findMany({ where: { orgId, companyId: { in: companyIds }, deletedAt: null }, select: {...}, take: 1000 })` — and that findMany has NO `orderBy`. For a key-account portfolio whose companies collectively own more than 1000 open/closed opportunities, the `take: 1000` cap truncates the set, so `totalValue`, `openDeals`, and `opportunityCount` in the response are silently wrong, and *which* rows survive the cap is non-deterministic (no ORDER BY) so the numbers also vary request-to-request. The helper `fetchAccountStats` (accounts.helpers.ts:30-47) carries the identical pattern and its doc comment only justifies the cap for the curated top-10 path (≤10 companies via TOP_ACCOUNTS_MAX), not the 200-company key list. This is exactly the class the MISTAKES ledger warns about (aggregate over an unbounded/under-bounded findMany). The /accounts/top auto path correctly pushes aggregation into a GROUP BY query; the key list does not.
confirmed.fix: Aggregate in Postgres for the key list too: replace the in-JS reduce over `opportunity.findMany` with a `groupBy({ by:['companyId'], _sum:{ valueMicros }, _count })` (or a $queryRaw GROUP BY like /accounts/top) so the totals are exact and bounded regardless of opportunity volume. If keeping findMany, at minimum add a deterministic orderBy and document/justify the truncation.

verdict.reason:
CONFIRMED at apps/api/src/routes/accounts.ts:94-119. The /accounts/key handler fetches up to `limit` companies (querystring `limit` max 200, default 50; lines 50, 81-92), then aggregates their opportunities with `prisma.opportunity.findMany({ where: { orgId, companyId: { in: companyIds }, deletedAt: null }, select: {...}, take: 1000 })` (lines 95-99). This findMany has NO `orderBy` — verified. The schema (packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:398-450) confirms Company→Opportunity is an unbounded one-to-many with no per-company cap. So if a single page of key-tier companies collectively owns more than 1000 non-deleted opportunities, the `take: 1000` truncates the set and the per-company loop (lines 110-119) silently undercounts totalValue/openDeals/opportunityCount. Because there is no ORDER BY, which 1000 rows survive is Postgres-arbitrary, so the truncated numbers can also vary request-to-request. This directly violates the project's own MISTAKES ledger rules (2026-05-30 and 2026-05-25): "Any findMany added to request paths must include an explicit, business-justified bound AND deterministic order." Note: the comparison /accounts/top auto path correctly pushes aggregation into a GROUP BY query (lines 245-279), so the asymmetry the claim describes is real.

CORRECTIONS to the claim: (1) The key route does NOT call the helper `fetchAccountStats` — it uses an inline copy of the aggregation (lines 94-119). `fetchAccountStats` (accounts.helpers.ts:30-47) carries the same `take: 1000` pattern, but it is only invoked from the /accounts/top CURATED branch (line 188), which is bounded to ≤10 companies (TOP_ACCOUNTS_MAX, line 185), so the helper's doc-comment safety rationale (lines 25-29) actually holds for its real caller. The only exposed instance is the inline copy in the key route. (2) Severity adjusted major→minor: the truncation only triggers when one page (default 50, max 200) of MANUALLY-FLAGGED key-tier strategic accounts collectively exceeds 1000 opportunities. Key accounts are typically dozens of regional strategic accounts, not hundreds, so real-world blast radius is small. The defect (missing orderBy + under-bounded aggregate) is genuine and worth fixing — ideally by switching the key route to the same GROUP BY pattern the top route already uses — but it is a tail-case correctness bug, not a routinely-hit major.

confirmed.title: dashboard.cockpit.ts is 673 lines (>400 budget) and buildCockpit is ~260 lines (>50 budget)
confirmed.evidence: code-quality.md hard floor: 'Max function length: 50 lines', 'Max file length: 400 lines'. The file is 673 lines. `export function buildCockpit({...})` spans lines 400–659 (~260 lines) in a single function body — KPI assembly, source-badge logic, risk/compliance filtering, contacts, roadmap all inline. The module header comment even self-reports buildCockpit as '~162 lines', which is already over the 50-line limit and is now understated.
confirmed.fix: Extract the KPI-block builder, the source-resolution helpers (externalField/fieldSource), and the risk/compliance selection into named helpers in the same module (or split serializers into a sibling file) so buildCockpit drops under 50 lines and the file under 400.

verdict.reason: Verified against the actual file and rule. apps/api/src/services/crm/dashboard.cockpit.ts is 673 lines (wc -l confirms 673), which exceeds the 400-line file budget in .claude/rules/code-quality.md line 41 ("Max file length: 400 lines (split if longer)"). The exported function buildCockpit spans lines 400-659 (closing brace at line 659; next section begins at line 661) = ~260 lines, far over the 50-line function budget in code-quality.md line 40 ("Max function length: 50 lines (refactor if longer)"). The body is a single monolithic transform: field-override application, company/opp filtering, Apollo source-badge logic (apolloSource/verifiedSource/missingApolloSource/externalField), risk and compliance filtering, KPI array assembly, contacts, recentActivity, and a hardcoded roadmap, all inline. confirmed.title: InfoSearch lead-intel endpoint has no read-permission gate — any authenticated user can pull PII for arbitrary account names
confirmed.evidence: GET /infosearch/leads is registered behind the global authPlugin but carries only `config.rateLimit` — no `preHandler: server.requirePermission(...)`. It accepts a free-text `account` query param and returns lead PII (name, company, title, phone, email, listName) from the external InfoSearch MCP, and also fires `notifyInfoSearchActivity` logging the caller. Every sibling mutation route in this wave gates on a permission (e.g. cross-sell.ts uses `requirePermission('accounts:write')`, accounts.ts read paths live under accounts scopes, user-groups.ts gates reads on `settings:read`). A low-privilege user who should not see commercial lead lists can enumerate them here by guessing account names. Note also fetchInfoSearchLeads (infosearch-client.ts:80-83) passes the raw account string to the MCP with no org binding, so results are not tenant-filtered by anything other than the upstream system.
confirmed.fix: Add `preHandler: server.requirePermission('accounts:read')` (or the nearest existing lead/intel read scope) to the route, matching the gating used on the other account-data surfaces; confirm the chosen scope is one a non-admin sales user legitimately holds.

verdict.reason: VERIFIED REAL. At D:\BIDCRM\apps\api\src\routes\infosearch.ts:30-53 the route GET /api/v1/infosearch/leads is registered with only `config: { rateLimit: { max: 30, timeWindow: '1 minute' } }` and a Zod schema — there is NO `preHandler`, no `server.requirePermission(...)`, no `server.requireRole(...)`. I confirmed the call chain has no other gate: the global authPlugin onRequest hook (apps/api/src/plugins/auth.ts:368-392) only AUTHENTICATES (sets req.auth with orgId/userId) and performs NO authorization; authorization in this codebase is strictly opt-in per route via the `requirePermission` preHandler (apps/api/src/plugins/rbac.ts:47-82). There is no default-deny layer. The handler accepts attacker-controlled free text (`account: z.string().trim().min(1).max(255)`) and returns PII: name, company, title, phone, email, listName (infosearch.ts:14-27, 42-44). It also fires notifyInfoSearchActivity logging req.auth.email. fetchInfoSearchLeads (infosearch-client.ts:80-83) forwards the raw account string to the external InfoSearch MCP as `query` with NO orgId binding, so results are bounded only by the upstream system — not by tenant. Suitable gate keys exist (leads:read, accounts:read, contacts:read in PERMISSION_KEYS), so the idiomatic fix (e.g. preHandler: [server.requirePermission('leads:read')]) is available. Net: any authenticated principal — including low-privilege roles and even a read-scoped API key (rbac.ts:50-53 lets role 'api' through on scope 'read') — can enumerate third-party commercial lead PII for arbitrary account names. ADVERSARIAL COUNTERPOINT (why not escalate to critical, and a correction to the claim's framing): the claim's assertion that 'every sibling read path gates on a permission' is overstated — sector-view.ts GET, cross-sell.ts GET /cross-sell-actions, and account-intel.ts GET all also lack requirePermission. So 'ungated read' alone is not a unique convention violation here. What genuinely distinguishes infosearch from those siblings, and makes the finding real rather than a style nit, is that those endpoints all scope queries by req.auth.orgId (tenant-bounded), whereas infosearch applies NO org scoping and queries an EXTERNAL PII database with free text. Exploitation requires an authenticated session (not unauthenticated), is rate-limited to 30/min, and the feature is flag-gated (infosearchConfigured() returns empty unless INFOSEARCH_ENABLED + URL + key are set), which is why I hold severity at 'major' rather than critical. confirmed.title: LMS course React keys can collide when courses lack ids — Sales Toolkits grid can drop/duplicate cards

confirmed.title: company_field_overrides rekey would fail / drop data on any non-empty table (acceptable now: no prod data, but a one-way data-loss migration)
confirmed.evidence: 001500 created the table with `company_id UUID NOT NULL` + a FK to companies. 001600 then runs `ALTER TABLE "company_field_overrides" DROP COLUMN "company_id", ADD COLUMN "company_key" TEXT NOT NULL;`. Two real risks: (1) DROP COLUMN company_id is a one-way data loss — any override rows created under 001500 lose their company linkage; (2) `ADD COLUMN ... TEXT NOT NULL` with NO DEFAULT and NO backfill UPDATE will hard-fail on a non-empty table (Postgres: 'column "company_key" contains null values'). Verified both migrations were committed together in 921293ce and never tagged/released, and grep found zero code still referencing the old company_id column, so on a fresh `db:reset` 001500 creates the table empty and 001600 alters zero rows = clean. Flagged per the lens instruction: this is safe ONLY because no environment ever applied 001500 with data. If 001500 had shipped to any persistent DB, 001600 would either error or silently destroy the company linkage with no migration audit of the loss.
confirmed.fix: Since this is pre-prod, prefer squashing 001500+001600 into a single migration that creates the table with company_key directly (eliminates the drop/data-loss step entirely). If the two-migration history must be preserved, the rekey should have been written as: ADD company_key as nullable, backfill via a join/UPDATE from companies, then SET NOT NULL — never a bare DROP + NOT NULL ADD.

verdict.reason:
Verified against the actual SQL and git history; the claim is accurate but the consequence is latent-only (never reachable in any environment), so it stays minor.

EVIDENCE CONFIRMED:
- D:\BIDCRM\packages\db\prisma\migrations\20260612001500_company_field_overrides\migration.sql lines 5 + 25: creates company_field_overrides with `company_id UUID NOT NULL` and an FK to companies.
- D:\BIDCRM\packages\db\prisma\migrations\20260612001600_field_overrides_company_key\migration.sql lines 11-12: `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN "company_id", ADD COLUMN "company_key" TEXT NOT NULL` with NO DEFAULT and NO backfill UPDATE. Exactly as cited.

Both Postgres risks in the claim are technically correct: (1) DROP COLUMN company_id is irreversible and would orphan the company linkage of any existing rows; (2) ADD COLUMN ... TEXT NOT NULL with no default and no backfill hard-fails on a non-empty table ("column \"company_key\" contains null values").

"SAFE NOW" CAVEAT ALSO CONFIRMED:
- git log shows both 001500 and 001600 were introduced in the SAME commit 921293ce (atomic — never an intermediate released state with only 001500 applied).
- Repo has ZERO tags (`git tag` returns nothing) — neither migration was ever tagged/released to a persistent DB.
- No code references the dropped company_id column on this model. schema.prisma lines 340-358 now key the model on `companyKey` (with a comment explaining the deliberate redesign: normalized company name, not a companies FK, because cockpit company identity spans enrichment UUIDs and opportunity-derived slugs). All API/service/test code (apps/api/src/routes/crm/companies.ts:262-279, dashboard.queries.ts, dashboard.service.ts, companies.test.ts) uses companyKey. On a fresh db:reset, 001500 creates the table empty and 001600 alters zero rows = clean.

VERDICT: The defect is real as a migration-craft hygiene issue (one-way rekey, no backfill, would fail/lose data on any non-empty table), but it is genuinely unreachable given the verified history — both migrations shipped atomically in one unreleased commit, no tags, no prod data. The claim's own framing ("acceptable now: no prod data") is accurate. Keeping severity at minor: it is a latent-only hazard, not an active defect, and is correctly downgradable to informational/cleanup. Worth a one-line backfill (e.g. populate company_key before the NOT NULL constraint, or squash the two dev-only migrations) if these ever risk reaching a persistent environment, but no fix is required for current safety.
